seoTitle: Truck Accident Lawyer in Ann Arbor, MI: I-94, US-23, and M-14 Interchanges, Campus Deliveries and Construction Trucks, University Vehicles in the Court of Claims, Charter Buses, the Federal Trucking Rules, and the Evidence That Expires
seoDescription: Hit by a semi, box truck, construction truck, or bus in Ann Arbor? 755 heavy trucks and buses were involved in Washtenaw County crashes in 2024, and 652 of the city’s crashes were on interstate routes. Learn how the federal trucking rules, the carrier’s $750,000-plus insurance, underride guards, Michigan no-fault, and the six-month Court of Claims notice for University vehicles apply, which agency owns the road, and why the logs must be preserved within days. Free review. (313) 406-7606.

Statewide, 110 people were killed and 3,613 injured in heavy truck and bus crashes. Ann Arbor recorded 2,770 crashes of all kinds, 652 of them on interstate routes and 163 on U.S. routes.

sections.heading: Where Ann Arbor truck crashes happen

c.v: I-94 on the city’s south side has interchanges at State Street, Ann Arbor-Saline Road, and Jackson Avenue, and the junction with US-23 to the east. The crashes are:

items.v: rear-end and underride crashes in the backups at the exit ramps, especially at State Street on football Saturdays and at the evening rush
lane changes into a car in the blind spot on the right side of the cab
trucks merging from short entrance ramps
fatigue crashes on overnight runs between Detroit and Chicago

c.v: A car that strikes the side or rear of a trailer can go under it. That is an

crash, which is often fatal or catastrophic. Trailers must carry rear impact guards that meet federal standards (49 CFR 393.86). A missing, damaged, or substandard guard is evidence against the carrier and the trailer’s owner.
US-23, M-14, and the Flex Route.

US-23 carries north-south freight past the city’s east side, and its junctions with I-94 to the south and M-14 to the north are where trucks and commuters merge at speed. North of the city, on the US-23 Flex Route, the left shoulder is opened as a travel lane at peak times. The crashes are:

items.v: merge crashes where lanes open and close
rear-end crashes in the slowdowns
crashes with vehicles stopped where the shoulder is in use

c.v: Work zones on US-23 and I-94 add lane shifts and narrowed shoulders. A work-zone crash can involve MDOT’s contractor as well as the truck.

Federal rules require a truck driver to use extreme caution in hazardous conditions, to reduce speed, and to stop if conditions become too dangerous (49 CFR 392.14). A jackknife or loss-of-control crash on an icy ramp or overpass is often a speed-for-conditions case.
Tractor-trailers and box trucks supply the shopping centers on State Street, Ellsworth, Washtenaw Avenue, and Jackson Avenue, and the research and office parks on the city’s edges. The crashes are:

items.v: wide right turns into a lot that catch a car, cyclist, or pedestrian on the inside of the turn
trucks backing into loading areas from the road
trucks stopped in a travel lane
trucks in the roundabout at State and Ellsworth, where a long trailer may need more than one lane

c.v: Campus and downtown: deliveries and construction.

Around the University and downtown, delivery trucks double-park, back into alleys, and turn across crowded crosswalks and bike lanes. Construction trucks, concrete mixers, and cranes serve a steady run of campus and hospital building projects. The crashes are:

items.v: right-turning trucks striking cyclists in a bike lane or pedestrians in a crosswalk; a truck’s blind spots are larger than a car’s
trucks backing into an alley or a site without a spotter
trucks stopped in a lane, forcing cars and cyclists around them
construction trucks entering and leaving sites across sidewalks

sections.heading: When the vehicle belongs to the University of Michigan

c.v: The University of Michigan is a constitutional state institution. A crash with a University-owned truck, maintenance vehicle, or bus is a claim against the State, under the motor vehicle exception to governmental immunity (MCL 691.1405). Three things change:

items.v: the claim is filed in the Michigan Court of Claims and decided by a judge, not a jury.
written notice, or the claim itself, must be filed within six months of the crash (MCL 600.6431). Missing it can end the claim.
the University’s coverage and self-insurance replace a carrier’s commercial policy, and the federal motor carrier insurance minimums generally do not apply to a government vehicle.

c.v: Every interstate carrier, and many Michigan intrastate carriers, has a USDOT number painted on the cab door. That number pulls up the carrier’s federal record:

items.v: (on the SAFER website) shows the carrier’s registered name and address, its number of trucks and drivers, and its inspections and crashes over the past two years, including out-of-service rates.

c.v: A poor record does not by itself prove fault in a crash. It can support a claim that the carrier failed to supervise or maintain its fleet, and that a shipper or broker was negligent in hiring a carrier with that record.

sections.heading: Who is responsible, and who pays

c.v: The motor carrier is responsible for its drivers’ compliance with the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations. It is liable for a driver’s negligence in the course of employment, and the driver can be sued as well. Michigan applies the federal rules to intrastate carriers (MCL 480.11a), so a local hauler that never leaves Washtenaw County is held to the same standards as an interstate carrier.

c.v: The owner of the truck or trailer.

In Michigan, a vehicle’s owner is liable for its negligent operation by someone driving with the owner’s consent (MCL 257.401). When the tractor, the trailer, and the driver belong to different companies, each may be a defendant, although a company in the business of renting or leasing vehicles is generally shielded from owner liability by federal law (49 USC 30106).
Michigan no-fault still applies to you.
Your own auto insurer, or a parent’s for a student who is still domiciled with them, pays these benefits regardless of fault (MCL 500.3107):

items.v: your medical bills, up to the PIP medical level on the policy

A pedestrian or cyclist with no household policy claims through the Assigned Claims Plan (MCL 500.3115).

Your claim against the driver and the carrier is for pain and suffering and for losses beyond no-fault, including medical bills above your PIP level. It requires a threshold injury (MCL 500.3135) and must be filed within three years (MCL 600.5805(2)). Michigan’s comparative fault rule concerns

faqs.question: How many truck accidents happen in Ann Arbor?

answer.v: The State’s county profile does not break out truck crashes by community. Countywide, 755 heavy trucks and buses were involved in Washtenaw County crashes in 2024. In the city, 652 crashes were on interstate routes and 163 on U.S. routes.

faqs.question: A semi changed lanes into me at the I-94 and State Street interchange. Who is at fault?

answer.v: Usually the truck driver, who must make sure a lane is clear before moving into it. A truck has large blind spots on its right side and directly behind the trailer. The truck’s dash camera and engine data are often the deciding evidence, and they are overwritten quickly.

faqs.question: A delivery truck turning right hit me on my bike near campus. Who is responsible?

answer.v: Usually the driver and the company that operates the truck, which may be a contracted delivery company rather than the store named on the package. A driver turning right must yield to a cyclist in the bike lane. Your no-fault benefits come from your household policy, or a parent’s, or the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan if there is none.

faqs.question: A University of Michigan truck or bus hit me. Is that different?

answer.v: Yes. The University is part of the State, so the claim goes to the Michigan Court of Claims, and written notice or the claim must be filed within six months of the crash. A private contractor’s truck working on a University project is a claim against the contractor in the ordinary courts.

faqs.question: I was hurt on a charter bus on a football Saturday. Who pays?

answer.v: Your no-fault benefits follow the bus-passenger rules. Your claim against the bus company, for pain and suffering and losses beyond no-fault, is against a federally regulated passenger carrier, which must carry at least $5 million in insurance for a bus seating 16 or more.

faqs.question: Do I have to prove the trucking company was more than 50 percent at fault?

answer.v: No. Michigan’s 50 percent rule concerns your own share of fault. If you were more than 50 percent at fault, you cannot recover pain-and-suffering damages. Every company that contributed to the crash can be named, whatever its share.

faqs.question: Is there a cap on what I can recover from a trucking company?

answer.v: Not on pain and suffering against the driver or carrier. Michigan’s damages caps apply to medical malpractice and product liability claims. In practice, the limit is the insurance available: the carrier’s policy, any excess policy, and your own underinsured coverage.

faqs.question: Why does the lawyer need to act within days?

answer.v: Because the records expire. Hours-of-service logs must be kept for six months and inspection reports for three. Camera footage lasts days or weeks. The truck’s electronic data and the trailer’s damage can disappear when the truck is repaired. And if a University vehicle was involved, the six-month notice is already running.
